title: TB6-06041
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Burundi, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated April 12, 2016, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Burundi, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated April 12, 2016, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA or the Act), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of Canada's protection. This appeal is dismissed.

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he fears returning to Burundi on account of his political opinion as a member of the opposition party: the Movement for Solidarity and Democracy (MSD). He joined the MSD party in 2009 and volunteered for the party. He attended party meetings and invited people to join the party. He began receiving anonymous telephone calls in 2012 telling him to contribute to the ruling party instead of the MSD party. On XXXX XXXX, 2012, the Appellant's brother was visiting the Appellant. His brother opened the door in response to knocks and was shot and killed. The Appellant believes that the men were pro-government militia and their intended target was the Appellant. The Appellant hid under a bed with his wife when the assailants entered the home searching for the Appellant's wife. The Appellant and his wife left their home and moved to a number of different locations from 2012 until they finally left Burundi. In 2015, the Appellant applied for and received his passport and Canadian visa on XXXX XXXX, 2015. The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2015, and the next day he was diagnosed with prostate cancer. He went to Maine, USA and stayed with his brother getting treatment for his cancer. He returned to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2015, and made an inland claim for refugee protection in November 2015.
This claim was heard by two sittings on January 20, 2016 and February 17, 2016. In rejecting this claim, the RPD found that the Appellant is not credible.
The Appellant did not submit new documents pursuant to section 110(4) of the IRPA to be considered as new evidence, and he is not requesting a hearing pursuant to section 110(6).

The Appellant argues that "this appeal should be allowed" and the decision of the RPD "should be set aside and the Appellant should be found to be a convention refugee or a person in need of protection; alternatively, the matter should be remitted to a different RPD Member..."
The minister intervened at the RPD hearing but did not do so at the RAD hearing.
The Appellant did not list his issues but argues that the RPD's credibility analysis is not correct. The Standard of Intervention
The Appellant submitted that the standard of review for the RPD's finding in this case should be correctness. The RAD agrees for the following reasons.

The scope of the appeal to the RAD is set out in Huruglica.1 The Federal Court in Huruglica stated that the RAD is to conduct its own independent assessment of the evidence and decide if the person is in need of refugee protection, and that the RAD is to show deference to RPD credibility findings and findings in areas where the RPD has a particular advantage (over the RAD).

The Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica2 regarding the Role of the RAD stated: [103] I conclude from my statutory analysis that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. No other interpretation of the relevant statutory provisions is reasonable. Credibility

The Appellant in the memorandum argues about the following five items raised by the RPD in its credibility findings and include: 1. MSD membership card; 2. Brother's death; 3. Appellant's children in Rwanda; 4. Police warrant; and 5. Visa Application to Canada.
As per Huruglica cited above, I will consider the Appellant's arguments on all these points and make my own determination after a thorough review of the record in. MSD Membership Card

The RPD found several inconsistencies between the description of the MSD party membership card in the objective documentary evidence and the card provided by the Appellant in support of his claim to the RPD. The RPD panel member considered the documentary evidence in detail and pointed out its concerns about the membership card in a cogent manner. The RPD provided sufficient opportunity to the Appellant to explain why his membership card does not conform to what is expected as per the objective documentary evidence. The RPD found the Appellant's explanations that he did not know was unreasonable. After a review of the evidence about the MSD party membership card, the RAD concurs with the RPD's finding and notes the following. Since the claim is entirely dependent on the Appellant's allegation regarding his activities with the MSD political party, it is not unreasonable for the Immigration and Refugee Board (Board) to expect the Appellant to be able to provide sufficient credible evidence for the Board to be able to make a finding that, on a balance of probabilities, he was a member of the party, and that his actions for the political party were perceived to be the governing party to target the Appellant. The Appellant's evidence does not do so.

In this case, the importance of party membership cards is further elevated because the Appellant knew at the time of making his claim that his wife's claim based on her membership in the same political party was denied due to the finding of the RPD that the cards did not conform to what was expected. In fact the Appellant stated in his Basis of Claim form narrative that "two major issues related to the fact that our membership cards did not conform to the information obtained by the immigration and refugee board of Canada.3"

The membership card provided by the Appellant to the RPD shows the issue date of XXXX XXXX, 2010.4 The card has six columns (years 2010 to 2015) and 12 rows (months - January to December). Intersection of rows and columns creates boxes where X's are marked from January 2010 to June 2015.

Objective documentary evidence (Response to Information Request (item 4.17, code: BDI104952.E) regarding the MSD membership card states that the current membership card is valid from January 2013 to December 2015 and its measurements are 8 by 10 centimetres. The party now has only one membership card identical everywhere in the country. The card is printed and has a four digit number printed on it. The unique feature of this card is the boxes for X marks; an "area reserved for a contributions schedule". Essentially an X mark is supposed to show that dues have been paid for that month. The documentary evidence also states that the current card is the third version replacing previous cards the first issued in August 2008 when the party did not enjoy official status as its name at that time was not approved. The party changed its name to gain official status in June 2009 and the party issued the second card with a five digit number. This card was valid until January 2013. Since 2013, the two old cards are neither distributed nor valid.

The card which has this unique feature of showing party contributions was not introduced until January 2013 and it was valid for three years. However the card provided by the Appellant shows contributions for six years; moreover the card was issued in XXXX XXXX, 2010 but this feature showing monthly party contributions did not appear until 2013. The Appellant had no explanation. It just doesn't make any sense that a political party would issue a card in 2010 which is not in circulation until 2013.

I also note that even if the card were XXXX and was issued prior to the 2010 elections, this card would be valid only until 2013, not from 2010 to 2015. Moreover, the card provided by the Appellant does not have the five digits number as it is supposed to have on the card.
The minister also pointed out that the card provided by the Appellant also does not meet the size measurements of 8 x 10 cm, it is larger.

The minister's submissions mention that all the X marks are consistent with respect to ink color and form.5 The RPD in its reasons noted the following regarding the X marks in the card presented by the Appellant to the RPD: Each "x" appears to be in generally the same form, used with the same colour of ink, and gives the appearance of all being filled in at the same time. The claimant testified that he does not know why, and the "x" was put on the schedule each time he made a contribution. He further testified that "the same pen was used each time". When asked by the Minister's counsel how he knows this to be true, the claimant testified that the same person marked each contribution and used the same pen "to prevent people from putting their own marks."

The RAD did not have the original card and therefore is unable to provide its own interpretation. This is one of the situations where the RPD enjoyed a particular advantage and therefore the RAD defers to the RPD's finding that the explanation provided by the Appellant was not reasonable.

The Appellant submits that the information provided from the Commune leader and the Secretary General of the MSD6 confirmed that membership cards that were issued in the South of Burundi did not necessarily match those issued in the rest of the country. I prefer objective documentary evidence over letters provided by other individuals which also contain information that is contradicted in the objective documentary evidence of the Board.

I have taken into consideration the profile of the Appellant as well. Documentary evidence states that "to obtain a membership card, a person must be considered a [translation] "strong and competent activist" and must be on the membership list.7" The MSD membership is restricted to "strong and competent activists." The activities the Appellant alleged he was doing for the party can hardly be considered worthy of a "strong and competent activist." Moreover, documentary evidence shows that the government is not out to get everyone associated with the party which has the following party staff:8 a) 1 president b) 1 secretary general c) 1 national coordinator d) 17 provincial representatives e) 129 communal representatives f) more than 1,200 representatives of neighbourhoods or zones g) more than 10,000 street representatives (MSD 19 July 2013).

The Appellant does not hold any of the offices listed above. Documentary evidence9 shows "The president of the MSD pointed out that the members of the MSD, in the commune of Ngagara, are victims of [translation] "constant intimidation." He stated that they are receiving threats and being interrogated for a few hours by the police before being released". He mentioned one commune not all over the country. There is no doubt that the party supporters may be harassed but there is no evidence to support the Appellant's allegation that the government is forcing people to financially support the governing party, otherwise they are persecuted.

Another document states:10 "although members of the MSD are not [translation] "afraid" of the regime in place, the contrary is true for the leader of the MSD, Alexis Sinduhije (28 Jan. 2013). According to PHW, Alexis Sinduhije is also the founder of the MSD." This document also states that a "spokesperson for the MSD, François Nyamoya, was arrested in September 2010 for having criticized the army, and he was imprisoned until October 2010." This is one month jail term for criticizing the government. The Appellant has done no such thing.

I also note that the affidavit of support from XXXX XXXX11 makes no mention of the Appellant facing any difficulty because of his political opinion or any other reason but states that he is a well-respected farmer and participates in community life solving conflicts and supporting local farmer organizations who work to improve their income, in addition to also being appointed as administrator of the local Pentecostal church.

Based on the foregoing, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's party membership card and supporting documents are not genuine. Party membership is at the core of this claim, and without establishing that he was a party member, there is insufficient credible evidence to find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. However, I have considered other issues as well. Appellant's brother's death

The Appellant provided a death certificate for the death of his brother who allegedly was visiting the Appellant at the time of his death. The Appellant is of the opinion that the assailants were targeting him and killed his brother by mistake. The Appellant's brother was allegedly killed on XXXX XXXX, 2012 but the death certificate was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2015 and it does not show the cause of death but states that he was shot. The Appellant could not explain why the death certificate was not issued until XXXX XXXX, 2015 and why there is no medical reasons for that rather than saying he was shot. The Appellant argues that being shot with a gun is sufficient explanation for the cause of death. I am not persuaded. A person may well be shot on the foot and suffer but is not likely to die because of the gunshot. I find the Appellant has not provided persuasive evidence of his brother's death or that he was killed by mistaken identity. The RPD's finding that "the documents submitted to corroborate the claimant's brother's death are lacking in credibility, on a balance of probabilities" is supportable. Appellant's children in Rwanda

Another issue in the Appellant's credibility determination was related to the registration of the Appellant's children in Rwanda. The Appellant arrived in Canada in XXXX 2015 and his wife did not arrive until XXXX 2015. The Appellant testified at the RPD hearing that he wished to ensure that their children were safely settled in Rwanda at a refugee camp. Thus, he left in XXXX after ensuring the children were registered with the United Nations High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) agency in Rwanda. The RPD noted that the UNHCR document show that the children were registered in Rwanda not in XXXX 2015 but were registered on XXXX XXXX, 2015. The Appellant's testimony in explanation was rather confusing and was not reasonable.

The Appellant argues in the memorandum that the facts that the children were registered in UNHCR confirm the Appellant's story and one of his friends helped with the registration process. The issue here was regarding the late departure of the Appellant's wife as she was remaining behind to ensure that the children were registered with the UNHCR in Rwanda. However she left more than a month before the date of registration. The issue is regarding contradiction between statements as to her staying behind to ensure registration and the fact that documents show that she left prior to the registration. This contradiction is not addressed by the Appellant in his arguments and thus remains unsolved. In addition the minister noted that the UNHCR proof of registration document lists nine people on the one household number, and five of these persons listed matched the list of the Appellant's children. It is not clear why the Appellant's friend would list the Appellant's children as his own; or why the Appellant's wife's name is not as the person helping with the registration. Based on the foregoing, I find that the RPD did not err in considering this issue in its credibility determination. Police warrant

The Appellant provided documents regarding police interest in the Appellant. The RPD extensively questioned the Appellant as to how and when he obtained these (since the Appellant had alleged that they were on the move since 2012) and noted in its reasons, that the Appellant "could not provide any context for the police documents such as where he got them, where they were issued in Burundi, and who got them."

The Appellant submitted that "The Board never addressed these documents as to from and the content of information contained on their face. Moreover, the Appellant was once again not in the country when the documents were issued and so the explanation that they contained his home address made sense since this was presumably the only address which the police had for the Appellant".

The central issue in this claim was his membership in the MDS political party and that was found to be not credible. The police document thus has to be considered for its credibility. It is not unreasonable for the RPD to expect the Appellant to be able to explain how this document came into his possession especially since he was in hiding and his house was without a roof and thus inhabitable. Thus questions such as to how the police delivered the document for the Appellant, to whom did they give this document and how the document was received by the Appellant, are all legitimate questions and the RPD did not err in considering these in its overall credibility analysis. Visa application to Canada

The RPD expressed concerns about the fact that the Appellant used his own home address to obtain his passport and the visa to Canada. The RPD's concern stemmed from the Appellant's testimony that the roof of their house was destroyed in 2012. The Appellant takes exception to the RPD reference to the house in its Reasons as "destroyed." I agree with the Appellant that it is not entirely correct to call the house without a roof as destroyed, however this error is not fatal to the RPD's decision. The Appellant's testimony was that the roof of his house was destroyed and the house was given to a supporter of the ruling party. Thus the issue is how the Appellant could get his passport as well as visa to Canada with that address. It just does not make sense. I am not persuaded that the RPD erred. I agree that the RPD could have chosen a different word to describe the house without a roof since 2012 in tropical weather in Burundi, Africa.

Moreover, the Appellant's son who appeared as a witness at the hearing and allegedly made all arrangements to obtain all the documents including the Appellant's MSD party membership related documents, could not provide a copy of the document "that he referred to as an 'attestation of proof of home address'" he used to obtain the Appellant's passport.

The RPD's reasons have to be considered in totality and not on a piece meal basis. As the Federal Court in Jakariya v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 1999 CanLII 8434 (FC) stated: For purposes of judicial review, however, it is my view that a Refugee Board's decision must be interpreted as a whole. One might approach it with a pathologist's scalpel, subject it to a microscopic examination or perform a kind of semantic autopsy on particular statements found in the decision. But mostly, in my view, the decision must be analyzed in the context of the evidence itself. I believe it is an effective way to decide if the conclusions reached were reasonable or patently unreasonable.
Even though the RAD is not doing the judicial review, I believe the court's direction applies here as well.

Mr. Justice Harrington commented in Owoussou v. M.C.I.,12 It would be grossly unfair to allow safe haven as a refugee simply on that person's say-so. Often, the core of the claim cannot be verified, but other elements can, which is why the rules call upon the claimant to provide acceptable documentation.

The RAD also notes that the Appellant's wife's claim was heard by another member, and in that case the Board also found the claimant (this Appellant's wife) was not credible. The Appellant before me had the advantage to consider the issues raised in his wife's claim and yet he did not address these to the satisfaction of the RPD or the RAD.

I note that the Federal Court of Appeal stated in Attakora:13 "Whether or not the applicant was a credible witness ... that does not prevent him from being a refugee if his political opinions and activities are likely to lead to his arrest and punishment." I do not have sufficient credible evidence that his political opinions and activities were such that there is a serious possibility of his arrest or punishment should he return to Burundi.
I find that there is insufficient credible evidence upon which to find that the Appellant is either a Convention refugee or a protected person.

The RAD having considered all of the issues raised by the Appellants and the evidence, confirms the determination of the RPD's decision pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the IRPA. The RAD finds that Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a persons in need of protection.

The RAD dismisses the appeal. (signed) "Atam Uppal" Atam Uppal June 22, 2016 Date 1 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93. 2 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v.
